goal_text: What to prepare when transitioning from SWE to AIPM

nodes.title: What does an AI PM actually do all day?
nodes.one_liner: The concrete job: decisions owned, artifacts produced, who they work with.

nodes.title: AI PM vs. SWE vs. standard PM
nodes.one_liner: How the role differs from your current job and from generic PM work.

nodes.title: Where your engineering background helps — and hurts
nodes.one_liner: SWE instincts that are leverage vs. ones that mislead you here.

nodes.title: Building product sense from scratch
nodes.one_liner: Judging user value, prioritization, and 'should we build this' beyond feasibility.

nodes.title: Why AI products are uncertain in ways software isn't
nodes.one_liner: Probabilistic outputs, eval, no guaranteed behavior, shifting model quality.

nodes.title: Data and model realities you'll own as PM
nodes.one_liner: Data availability, labeling, model lifecycle, and their product tradeoffs.

nodes.title: Working with researchers, data scientists, and stakeholders
nodes.one_liner: New collaboration dynamics, expectation-setting, and managing nontechnical execs.

nodes.title: Is this transition actually for you?
nodes.one_liner: Honest fit check: what you'd gain, give up, and need to enjoy.

outline.rationale: The user is a SWE exploring whether to become an AI PM, wanting a conceptual working understanding rather than tactical job-search prep. I excluded basics of ML/APIs (they can absorb fast), résumé/portfolio, and 90-day plans per the confirmed understanding. The outline centers on the conceptual shift: a grounding node on what the role concretely is, a comparison node positioning it against SWE and standard PM, a leverage-vs-liability node specific to their engineering background, then three genuinely-new skill areas the understanding flagged (product sense, AI-specific uncertainty, data/model realities), a stakeholder/collaboration node, and a closing fit-assessment node matching their 'is this for me' framing. Nodes are MECE-ish — the role definition, the comparison, the background audit, and the distinct skill domains have low overlap. Ordered so foundational understanding precedes skill-building and the fit decision comes last.
